introduction: These hundred readings describe the human soul: the rational soul that sets a person apart from the animal, discovers what the senses cannot reach, begins with each life and does not end with the body, and grows or is stunted by what a person chooses. They also say that its essence cannot be known. Beside them stand passages from scriptures and from thinkers who said similar things, among them Plato's likeness of the divine, the chariot of the Katha Upanishad, the spirit that returns to God who gave it, and the Qur’an's soul that grows or is stunted. Others disagree at important points: Hume, who looked within and found no self; Darwin on degree and kind; Lucretius on death; Plato and Wordsworth on a soul that existed before; the Upanishad's rivers that forget their names in the sea.
questions: The readings say the soul's essence cannot be known, only its signs. What signs of a soul do you recognize in yourself and in others?
Hume looked within and found only passing perceptions. What do you find when you look, and what does that show?
Darwin held that the human mind differs from the animal in degree, not kind; the readings say in kind. Which human capacities seem to you decisive?
The readings hold that each soul has a beginning and no end, against Plato's many births and the river that forgets itself in the sea. What turns on keeping an individual identity?
The Qur’an says a person succeeds who causes the soul to grow. What, in practice, makes a soul grow, and what stunts it?
One reading calls self and passion the true prison. What has helped you out of it?

outside.why: Aristotle held that reason, more than anything else, is man, and that the life according to reason is therefore best for him.
Elihu says in the Book of Job: there is a spirit in man, and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding.
Jesus spoke at the well of a water that becomes, in the one who drinks it, a well of water springing up.
Robert Browning's Paracelsus says that truth is within ourselves and takes no rise from outward things.
Through Jeremiah God promises to put His law in their inward parts and write it in their hearts.
Wordsworth wrote that the soul that rises with us comes from afar, trailing clouds of glory from God, who is our home. Is a child's purity a memory of somewhere else, or a beginning?
Locke supposed the mind at birth to be white paper, furnished afterwards by experience. If the soul begins pure, where does its later character come from?
The Qur’an says: they ask thee concerning the Spirit; say, the Spirit is by command of my Lord, and of knowledge ye have been vouchsafed but little.

David Hume reported that when he looked most intimately into what he called himself, he found only some perception or other, and never a self. What would you say to someone who looks within and finds no soul?
Paul says that the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit, for they are spiritually discerned.
Plato's Socrates passes on a teaching that the soul is immortal, has been born again many times and has seen all things. What does it change to hold that each soul has a beginning?
Paul prays that the whole spirit and soul and body of his friends be preserved blameless.
The Letter to the Hebrews says that the word of God pierces even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit.
Proverbs says: keep thy heart with all diligence, for out of it are the issues of life.
Alexander Pope placed man on an isthmus of a middle state, in doubt to deem himself a god or beast. Is standing between two worlds a privilege or a predicament?
Emily Dickinson wrote that the brain is wider than the sky, for put them side by side, the one the other will include.
Pascal said that it is not from space that he must seek his dignity, but from the government of his thought.
Paul says that the Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit that we are the children of God.
Jesus told Nicodemus that what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.
The Bhagavad Gita says: let each man raise the Self by Soul, not trample down his Self.
The Katha Upanishad says: know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot, the intellect the charioteer, and the mind the reins.
The psalmist says: I am fearfully and wonderfully made, and that my soul knoweth right well.
Proverbs calls the spirit of man the candle of the Lord, searching all the inward parts.
Shakespeare's Cassius tells Brutus that he cannot see himself so well as by reflection. If the soul cannot comprehend itself, by what reflections does it come to know what it is?
Aristotle begins his Metaphysics with the words: all men by nature desire to know.
Plato held that the power of learning exists in the soul already, and that the whole soul must be turned toward the light.

Darwin concluded that the difference in mind between man and the higher animals, great as it is, is one of degree and not of kind. What evidence would settle whether the difference is of degree or of kind?
John Stuart Mill wrote that it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied.
Keats compared a discovery of the mind to a watcher of the skies when a new planet swims into his ken.
Francis Bacon wrote that knowledge and power meet in one, and that nature to be commanded must be obeyed.
A chorus of Sophocles sings that wonders are many, and none is more wonderful than man.
The psalmist says that man has been made a little lower than the angels and crowned with glory and honour.
The Letter to the Hebrews calls faith the evidence of things not seen.
Kant said that two things fill the mind with ever new admiration and awe: the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
The Qur’an challenges men and jinn to penetrate the regions of the heavens and the earth, if they are able.
Jesus said that the light of the body is the eye, and if the eye be single the whole body shall be full of light.
Walt Whitman called himself an acme of things accomplished and an encloser of things to be: still I mount and mount.

In Stephen Crane's poem a man says to the universe, Sir, I exist, and the universe replies that the fact creates in it no sense of obligation. How does the greatness these readings claim for the human spirit look from there?
Leibniz held that each simple substance is a perpetual living mirror of the universe.
Marcus Aurelius asked his reader to regard the universe as one living being, having one substance and one soul. Does the soul that contains all creation belong to each person, or to the whole?
The psalmist says that his substance was not hid from God when he was made in secret.
Zechariah speaks of the Lord who stretches forth the heavens and formeth the spirit of man within him.
Through Ezekiel God says: behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine.
Jesus spoke of a woman in travail, who remembers the anguish no more for joy that a man is born into the world.
Rabbi Jacob said that this world is like a vestibule before the world to come: prepare yourself in the vestibule.
Paul says that we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the power may be of God.
Genesis says that God breathed into man's nostrils the breath of life, and man became a living soul.
In the Qur’an God says of the first man: when I have made him and have breathed into him of My Spirit.
Rumi wrote: I died as inanimate matter and arose a plant, I died as a plant and rose again an animal, I died as an animal and arose a man.
Emerson wrote that, striving to be man, the worm mounts through all the spires of form. Is the growth of the spirit a climb by the creature or a gift to it?
Plato's Socrates concludes that the soul is in the very likeness of the divine, immortal and indissoluble, and the body in the likeness of the mortal.
The Bhagavad Gita says: never the spirit was born; the spirit shall cease to be never.
Lucretius argued that death is nothing to us, for when the body is dissolved there is no one left to suffer. What reasons do you find for thinking that the mind outlasts the body?
Paul says that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God.
Prospero says that we are such stuff as dreams are made on, and our little life is rounded with a sleep.
Jesus said: fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.
Paul says that though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
The Preacher says that the dust shall return to the earth as it was, and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.
The same Preacher says elsewhere that man has no preeminence above a beast, for all have one breath. Which of his two sayings does experience support?
In the parable God says to the man with full barns: this night thy soul shall be required of thee.
Proverbs says that the spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity, but a wounded spirit who can bear?
Seneca called the day we fear as the end of all things the birthday of our eternity.
Paul says that now we see through a glass, darkly, but then face to face.

Hamlet calls what follows death the undiscovered country from whose bourn no traveller returns, and says the dread of it puzzles the will. Is not being able to describe that condition a reason for dread, or for trust?
Paul says that eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, the things which God hath prepared.
The first letter of John says: it doth not yet appear what we shall be.
The psalmist looks at the heavens and asks: what is man, that Thou art mindful of him?
Paul prays that the eyes of his friends' understanding may be enlightened.
Asked about death, Confucius answered: while you do not know life, how can you know about death? How much attention should the next plane receive from those still on this one?
The Book of Daniel says that they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and as the stars for ever.
In John's Gospel Jesus says: this is life eternal, that they might know Thee, the only true God.
The Chandogya Upanishad says that rivers, once they are in the sea, do not know I am this or that river. Is the soul's goal to keep its individual consciousness or to lose it?
Paul says that there is one glory of the sun and another of the moon, and one star differeth from another star in glory.
The Qur’an says of the soul: he is indeed successful who causeth it to grow, and he is indeed a failure who stunteth it.
The first letter to Timothy says that bodily exercise profiteth little, but godliness is profitable unto all things.
Plato pictures the soul as a charioteer driving a pair of horses, one noble and one not.
A character in Dostoevsky says that God and the devil are fighting, and the battlefield is the heart of man. Is the struggle between higher and lower in us a war, or a matter of education?
Paul confesses: the good that I would I do not, but the evil which I would not, that I do.
Moses says: I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life.
Ezekiel says that when the wicked man turneth away from his wickedness and doeth what is right, he shall save his soul alive.
The psalmist says: bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all His benefits.
Paul says that that which is natural comes first, and afterward that which is spiritual.
The Dhammapada says: self is the lord of self; who else could be the lord? Who frees a person from the prison of self: the self, or a power beyond it?
Mencius said that people know to seek their lost fowls and dogs, but lose their mind and do not know to seek for it.
Gerard Manley Hopkins wrote that this Jack, joke, poor potsherd is immortal diamond.
Augustine says to God that our hearts are restless until they rest in Thee.
The psalmist says that his soul pants after God as the hart pants after the water brooks.
Jesus said: blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
Nietzsche called man a rope stretched between the animal and the Superman, a rope over an abyss. How does growth toward the spirit differ from the self-overcoming he had in mind?
The elder wishes his friend to prosper and be in health, even as his soul prospereth.
Mary's song begins: my soul doth magnify the Lord, and my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.
The psalmist says that his soul waits for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning.
The psalmist says: return unto thy rest, O my soul, for the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee.
Montaigne observed that there is more ado to interpret interpretations than to interpret things. How much of the difficulty about soul, spirit and mind lies in the words?
Thoreau asked: am I not partly leaves and vegetable mould myself? What is gained and what is lost by thinking of ourselves as wholly of the earth?
Pope wrote of a vast chain of being that runs from infinite to man, and from man to nothing.
Wordsworth felt a motion and a spirit that impels all thinking things and rolls through all things.
Jesus said that the wind bloweth where it listeth, and so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
Jesus asked what it shall profit a man if he gain the whole world and lose his own soul.
The Qur’an addresses the soul at peace: return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure.

thessalonians-spirit-and-soul-and-body.text: And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ

psalm-bless-the-lord-o-my-soul.text: Bless the Lord, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits

zechariah-formeth-the-spirit-of-man.text: saith the Lord, which stretcheth forth the heavens, and layeth the foundation of the earth, and formeth the spirit of man within him

psalm-my-soul-waiteth.text: I wait for the Lord, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope. My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning

luke-soul-doth-magnify.text: My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour

psalm-return-unto-thy-rest.text: Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee

ezekiel-all-souls-are-mine.text: Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die

proverbs-spirit-of-a-man-sustain.text: The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a wounded spirit who can bear

plato-soul-likeness-of-the-divine.text: the soul is in the very likeness of the divine, and immortal, and intelligible, and uniform, and indissoluble, and unchangeable; and the body is in the very likeness of the human, and mortal, and unintelligible, and multiform, and dissoluble, and changeable
plato-soul-likeness-of-the-divine.author: Plato

plato-soul-born-many-times.text: The soul, then, as being immortal, and having been born again many times, and having seen all things that exist, whether in this world or in the world below, has knowledge of them all
plato-soul-born-many-times.author: Plato
